cim: A view of artificial intelligence from within Spokane's tech industry
cim_eredeti: A view of artificial intelligence from within Spokane's tech industry
szoveg_eredeti:
Many who work in the tech industry are bullish about artificial intelligence and its future. Some have concerns.

We get the views of two people who work within Spokane's tech industry.

Clayton Gravatt is a data and AI architect at IntelliTect, which is a financial supporter of Spokane Public Radio. Dan Olvera is a software engineer there.

DN: How would you explain to folks older like me about the benefits of artificial intelligence and maybe your concerns about it?

Clayton Gravatt: Benefits of AI. As with any powerful tool, when used wisely, AI is awesome for automating the things that you don't want to have to do by hand. It's also potentially risky in that it's very, very easy and tempting to hand over your thinking to AI in a lot of places.

Navigating that line of how do I give AI more access and involve it more in my processes so that they can go faster and I can focus on more of the things that I care about, that'd be the benefit, but not so much of the control over the system that I don't know what's going on or AI has even the capability of making permanent mistakes that negatively affect people.

Dan Olvera: And I think when you talk about concerns for AI, there's kind of two major things. There's what AI can do, and then the effects of AI.

So economic effects and displacement of workers is a major concern. As technical people, we're more on the other side of it. When AI has access, what is it doing with that data? So whether it's leaking data or it's finding holes where you didn't think there were, that's kind of where we have more expertise in the concerns.

I think there are broader concerns that are more widespread. What does people's sentiment around AI lead to at an economic standpoint? But yeah, I think our concerns, and at least my expertise where we do our pros and cons is around how much data do you give it access to and what capabilities? So read and write, very different. If it can read systems, especially if it's not confidential data, there's little risk.

But as soon as you put confidential data or writing systems or being able to delete things, that's when you get to be a lot more judicious about how you expose your data. And so enterprises are grappling all over the place with, okay, what systems do we enable and flip on all these AI switches? And then there's the capabilities as well. What are they doing within those systems?

DN: Are there places that you consciously in your own lives choose not to stay away from AI?

CG: Definitely. So in interactions with my son, so I have a one-year-old son and I love spending time with him and reading books to him. And I've seen articles on the internet of people saying, oh, I've created this app that will read my children their bedtime stories. And to me that, sure, it's automating the function that I'm providing of reading out the story, but it loses that human connection that's really the driving value behind it. I'm not reading a book to my son for him just to hear the words, I'm doing it to connect with him.

So that human level of connection is something that I am very cognizant about not replacing with AI whenever I can.

DO: I think the other major piece is like the creative aspect, right? I do a lot of writing. Obviously, you know, in school, writing was never my strongest suit, but I really liked writing.

And then in college, you know, you do lots of technical writing courses and technical writing can be, you know, a lot of people use AI. That's one of the major, it's like the top three use cases of AI within the business right now is writing. And then research is up there as well.

But then creative writing is a very different thing to me. So like, if I'm doing that on the weekend, why am I offloading something that I'm choosing to engage with for fun to AI, right? Then that removes and it results in a lot of things that like I'm not connected to as well. So anything you want to have like, kind of like an intimate connection to should be done by yourself, at least in my opinion.

DN: I love AI for turning audio. This interview after we're done is going to go into an AI generator of some kind, and it's going to create within a couple of minutes, a transcript so I don't have to spend an hour or an hour and a half transcribing it myself. What are some of the other most useful, less dangerous uses of AI that people might ask you about that you say, this is what AI is meant to be and it's perfect for?

CG: Oh man, anything where it's easy to verify the results, verify it was done correctly.So something like a transcript is something where you heard the interview yourself and you can quickly review that transcript. I think that's a great use case for it.So summarization, helping you understand material, helping you do research, especially when AI is giving you links to things, for example, and you are then verifying afterwards of yourself. Any of those.

DO: We do timekeeping as consultants. So I go and track my time. I have a calendar that says, here's my meetings. I kind of know what I'm doing throughout the day. And then you have to write descriptions because then that is part of what you build a client. Writing those descriptions and pulling from a calendar and looking at all my time, I have to go to four different systems to do that, especially if I'm on multiple different clients or whatever. So things that are like administrivia, I feel like a lot of times can be leveraged with AI.

DN: As you guys continue your careers and as AI has developed so rapidly, how do you keep up with what's going on in AI so that you feel like you're constantly current and can help the clients that you work with?

CG: For me, I dedicate time every day. I start my morning with making sure I keep up on the latest developments, but there are so many that I cannot keep up on everything.

So I've developed an area of expertise, a set of tools that I am most interested in, and I'm sure to read in depth about those whenever those update. And I am tangentially aware of what else is going on in the world, but I'm intentionally not becoming an expert on those other pieces that I've become disinterested in.

DO: And I think the other part of that is because it's changing so rapidly, everyone feels behind and that's almost like a feature, not a bug of the system, where because you feel behind, then you don't need to go invest and put money into it and that's just because companies are trying to one-up each other, right?

So pick your niches and pick where your strengths are and focus there on developments or new things and new features that come out. Because as things continue to go, lots of things are gonna go by the wayside, right? We're gonna find the better ways to leverage AI, right?

Ten years ago, everyone was like, oh, we're gonna use voice chat all the time with our phones. And it was terrible and everyone hated it and you looked like, oh, this is not working anymore. So then it kind of fell by the wayside. And now it's like coming back, but there's a lot of things that people are trying out, but not necessarily going to stick around for a long time.

DN: So is it your job to help companies wade through all of that and determine how quickly should I be adopting, or should I just leave this alone and wait for a while until the bugs are worked out, so to speak?

DO: Depends on the role, right? Some companies can do that, right? They're the more agile, they want to be at the front lines and experiencing things. Other companies aren't, they're a financial institution, they're not gonna be picking up the latest thing just because it looks cool, right? They're gonna move slowly, they have more regulations. And that's a good thing, right? They should be picking up the things that are tried and true. So yeah, definitely depending on the role.
